requirements.requirement: Establish /etc/inventory/app.conf on node1 as the authoritative source of truth
requirements.summary: Executor created /etc/inventory/app.conf on node1 with real content and captured its checksum; content was directly read back in the same command.

requirements.requirement: Maintain a synchronized copy of the file on node2 that matches node1
requirements.summary: A root-run pull script (ssh+sudo cat, atomic mv) was created on node2, manually executed, and shown to produce a byte-identical copy of node1's file (matching checksum and content).

requirements.requirement: Automatically propagate a change on node1 to node2 within 15 minutes without manual intervention
requirements.summary: A root crontab entry runs the sync script every 5 minutes. After editing node1's file, journalctl on node2 showed the cron job autonomously firing (12:35:01, well under the 15-minute bound) and updating the file; a follow-up diff against node1 confirmed the files were identical.

requirements.requirement: Sync mechanism continues to function (survives normal operational disruption such as a reboot)
requirements.summary: Baselines were captured on both nodes before reboot (boot_id, uptime, service state, matching checksums, installed crontab). Both nodes were rebooted (native `sudo reboot`), polled until reachable, and boot_id/uptime were confirmed changed on each, with sshd/crond active afterward and the config file and cron entry intact. A further post-reboot edit on node1 was picked up autonomously by node2's cron (journalctl showing a 12:40:01 firing) with matching checksums, directly demonstrating recovered, functioning sync behavior across a bounded disruption.

overall_summary: The executor established node1's /etc/inventory/app.conf as source of truth and built a working one-way pull sync (SSH-key based, root cron every 5 minutes) to node2. End-to-end propagation was directly verified twice via autonomous cron firings recorded in journalctl with matching checksums/diffs, well within the 15-minute requirement. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was also executed on both nodes with full pre/post boot-identity, service, and data verification, and the sync mechanism was shown to still work correctly after both reboots. Hygiene is good with only minor leftover /tmp log files as residue.
limitations: Sync interval (5 minutes) was verified twice via real firings; longer-run stability over many cycles was not observed, though this is sufficient to establish the mechanism works within the required 15-minute bound.

Two commands (cmd-09c7eb7a4c764a01, cmd-f556e779cdc54b14) hit proxy timeouts during polling waits; these were immediately followed by successful direct checks that captured the needed state, so they do not affect the conclusions.

Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) on both nodes at both snapshots, so package-manager consistency could not be independently confirmed, though no other evidence suggests package damage.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace to a clear purpose: creating the source file, establishing SSH trust (keypair, authorized_keys, /etc/hosts, known_hosts), writing/replacing the sync script (the first version was superseded by a working root-capable version with no separate residue since the same path was overwritten), installing the cron entry, and the reboot cycle mandated by the provider-wide restart protocol (fully recovered on both nodes). No destructive, broad, or security-weakening mutations were found, and the temp-file handling inside the sync script uses mktemp with a cleanup trap. Minor residue: /tmp/reboot.log and /tmp/sync-inventory-conf.err were left on node2 (and /tmp/reboot.log on node1) per the lifecycle diff — low-risk log artifacts in /tmp, not cleaned up after the reboot protocol and one earlier fetch failure.
